violated_invariant: Only proposals genuinely approved by the DAO's Reality oracle process may be executed through the Safe module; the bond requirement and dispute window must make a bogus answer uneconomic.
notes: The Gnosis SafeSnap-style DaoModule lets anyone add a proposal and, because the module was deployed with a zero minimum bond (the `minBond == 0 ||` branch in executeProposalWithIndex skips the bond check) and only a 24h cooldown, the attacker answered their own Reality question with a 1 wei bond and executed mint/transferOwnership calls through the Safe. This is a governance-design/parameter weakness in otherwise standard module code rather than a classic coding error; the two timestamp findings (18, 19) sit in the execution path but flag block.timestamp use, not the missing bond/dispute protection, so nothing explains the exploit. Other candidates (RNBW, LPOP, PrimaryBridge, Realitio) are affected targets or the oracle, not the defect.

violated_invariant: Only an authorised minter may increase the token supply.
notes: Token.mint() is public with no modifier or caller check and mints a fixed 1e17 units to msg.sender, so the attacker simply called it and dumped the tokens into the Uniswap V3 pool. The only finding on mint() is too-many-digits (index 4), which comments on the literal, not the missing access control, so it does not explain the exploit; the remaining findings are dead inlined-OpenZeppelin code and compiler-version noise. The two UniswapV3Pool candidates are the drained venues, not defects.

violated_invariant: Redeeming N vault shares may pay out at most N shares' pro-rata portion of vault assets, with decimals/price state read from the slots the logic was written against.
notes: The victim address is a TransparentUpgradeableProxy and only the proxy/OZ sources were recovered; the exploited logic lives in the upgraded EFVault implementation, whose storage layout shifted relative to the proxy's existing state so the share-to-asset conversion in redeem() read a wrong (decimals/price) slot and paid ~5.1M USDC for 676,562 shares. The location names are taken from the PoC and public analyses, not from recovered source, hence medium confidence. All 36 proxy findings are OpenZeppelin library noise except the shadowing-local on the wrapper constructor (21), which is harmless; none touches the implementation, so nothing can explain a storage-layout bug Slither would need the implementation (and its upgrade history) to see.

violated_invariant: yUSDT share price must reflect only USDT-denominated holdings in the configured lending venues; a vault's constant iToken address must be the one matching its underlying.
notes: The legacy yUSDT iEarn vault was deployed with the Fulcrum address pointing at iUSDC rather than iUSDT, so its balance/share-price accounting counted a token it should never hold; the attacker used flash loans and Aave repayments to steer the APR recommender, donated iUSDC to inflate the share price, withdrew the real USDT, rebalanced the emptied vault and then minted huge yUSDT against 1 wei, dumping it into the Curve y-pool. I label the defect as a misconfigured constant (`other`) with a secondary business-logic failure (share price derived from manipulable/donated balances). The prepared file contains only the Aave debtor addresses with no source, so there are no Slither findings to adjudicate; victim_addresses is the yUSDT address from the PoC.

violated_invariant: Only the project owner may move a third party's token balance or call an arbitrary router with the contract's tokens; a user's balance may only decrease through transfers they authorise.
notes: VINU.addLiquidityETH is external and unrestricted: it takes caller-chosen router, LP-receiver and `devaddr` arguments, moves 80% of `devaddr`'s balance into the token contract, then calls the caller's router. The attacker passed the Uniswap pair as devaddr with a dummy router, repeatedly stripped VINU out of the pair, synced the reserves and sold into the distorted price. The two unused-return findings (11, 12) are on the defective function but describe ignored router/approve return values, not the missing access control or untrusted address parameters, so they do not explain the exploit; they, the shadowing-local pair and the reentrancy-no-eth on _transfer (external call to an owner-set router before balance updates) are real but minor. The UniswapV2Pair candidate is the affected venue; its findings are left unresolved.

violated_invariant: The omnipool's LP exchange rate must value its Curve LP positions at a price consistent with the price at which it actually adds/removes liquidity in the same transaction, so a deposit-then-withdraw round trip cannot extract value.
notes: The crvUSD omnipool mints and burns its LP token at an exchange rate computed from controller.priceOracle().getUSDPrice(curveLpToken) in _curveLpToUnderlying, while the actual Curve add/remove liquidity executes at the pools' current (attacker-skewed) balances; by flash-borrowing crvUSD, pushing the crvUSD/USDC and crvUSD/USDT pools off peg and sandwiching deposit/withdraw cycles the attacker turned the gap between oracle valuation and execution value into profit. The oracle contract itself is not among the candidates, so medium confidence on the exact split of blame. None of the 316 findings concerns oracle trust: the reentrancy-balance hits on depositFor/withdraw (255-258) flag ERC20 transfers of crvUSD, which has no hooks, and the incorrect-equality/uninitialized-local/unused-return hits are the usual `== 0` guard, memory-struct and mint/burn-return noise, so none explains the exploit.

violated_invariant: An account can withdraw at most what it (or its alt) actually deposited; alt-account withdrawals must debit the correct balance and never create withdrawable credit out of nothing.
notes: From the PoC alone: the attacker deposits 2 USDT/USDC, has a helper contract call lockTokens(attacker, 0) to register the attacker as its alt account, then calls withdrawTokensWithAlt(token, helper, 1e6), after which the helper can call withdrawTokens for the contract's entire token balance. That pattern indicates the alt-account withdrawal path mis-credits or fails to debit balances (a bookkeeping bug combined with unchecked alt/lock parameters) rather than a missing owner check. The victim contract has no recovered source and no Slither output, so no findings can be adjudicated and confidence is low on the exact defect line.

violated_invariant: When a swap moves the price exactly onto or across an initialised tick boundary, that tick must be crossed and the liquidity range updated; the swap-step arithmetic must not let the computed price land a hair short of the boundary while the quantities assume it was reached.
notes: The attacker flash-loaned, drove the pool price into a thin range, minted a concentrated position and then swapped so that the step arithmetic in SwapMath (computeSwapStep/calcReachAmount/calcFinalPrice) produced a final sqrt price just short of the tick boundary while the quantities were computed as if it had been reached; Pool.swap's boundary check therefore skipped the tick crossing, liquidity was double-counted and the pool paid out far more than it held. Slither's divide-before-multiply and incorrect-exp hits (13-22) are the well-known false positives on FullMath.mulDiv's modular-inverse and TickMath's fixed-point ladder, not the tick-crossing precision flaw in SwapMath/Pool.swap, so none explains the exploit. The reentrancy-no-eth and uninitialized-local hits are noise (trusted oracle calls, memory structs). The AntiSnipAttackPositionManager candidate is periphery, not the defect.

violated_invariant: collectInterest may only pull interest from registered staking contracts, and no external call made during interest collection may re-enter the reserve's buy/sell path before the collection's accounting completes.
notes: GoodFundManager.collectInterest takes a caller-supplied array of staking contracts and calls collectUBIInterest on each without checking they are registered; the attacker's fake staking contract re-entered the GoodReserve (GDX) buy path during that callback, after flash-loaning WETH and borrowing cDAI, so G$ were bought/minted at a stale reserve state and later sold back for DAI. Only the ERC1967 proxy/ProxyFactory1967 source was recovered for the victim (and for the reserve 0xa150...), not the GoodFundManager implementation, so the function names come from the PoC and public analyses. Every finding on the proxy candidate concerns the factory's assembly, naming and events and has nothing to do with the forwarded logic, so none explains the exploit; the GoodDollar token, cETH, cDAI and Unitroller candidates are affected third-party contracts and their findings are left unresolved.

violated_invariant: Only the holder of (or an account authorised for) the vault's BUI SetToken shares may redeem them, and redemption proceeds must go to that holder, not an arbitrary receiver.
notes: The PoC's whole attack is one call: redeem(BUI.balanceOf(victim), attacker) on the unverified SoulMate contract, which burns the contract's entire BUI SetToken holding and sends the underlying USDC/DAI/MATIC/AAVE/ENS/ZRX/UNI to the caller-chosen receiver, so the defect is a missing caller/ownership check on redeem with an unvalidated receiver. The victim has no recovered source, so no Slither output exists for it; the SetToken, Matic, Aave proxy, ENS and ZRX candidates are the redeemed basket and its components (third-party, not the defect), so their findings are left unresolved. Medium rather than high because the exact internal logic of redeem is inferred from the transaction effect, not read.
